draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated sentence being said by seven different people?"}
review: The question is reasonable but presupposes that each visible repetition is a separate utterance and that “people” is the relevant distinction. The sentence could be repeated by one person (e.g., an echo, recording, ritual, or multiple occasions), or the formatting could itself matter. Ask instead: “In the story, are the seven instances intended as seven distinct spoken utterances occurring at the same time?” This cleanly tests both the utterance assumption without committing to seven speakers.
action: {"type":"question","text":"In the story, are the seven instances intended as seven distinct spoken utterances occurring at the same time?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven repeated lines meant to represent the same utterance being repeated over time, rather than seven different utterances?"}
review: The proposal largely revisits the answered question: “not seven distinct utterances at the same time” does not establish that they are one utterance repeated over time. The repetition could instead be written text, echoes, multiple speakers, a counting/formatting device, or something else. Avoid presupposing a temporal repetition. A better discriminating question is: “Does the repeated line’s multiplicity itself have an in-story cause or significance?” If asking about chronology is useful, phrase it neutrally: “Are the seven appearances associated with seven separate moments in the story?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the fact that the line appears seven times have an in-story cause or significance?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven repetitions caused by a written or recorded message being reproduced, rather than by the speaker deliberately saying the sentence seven times?"}
review: The question is reasonable but embeds an unsupported binary: the repetitions may have significance without being a written/recorded message, and “reproduced” could cover several distinct mechanisms. The prior “no” only rules out seven distinct utterances occurring simultaneously; it does not establish that the line is mechanically reproduced. A better discriminating question is: “Is the repeated presentation primarily caused by how the line is being displayed or heard, rather than by seven separate utterances in the story?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated presentation primarily caused by how the line is being displayed or heard, rather than by seven separate utterances in the story?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the same person saying this line repeatedly on seven different occasions, with each repetition referring to a separate departure?"}
review: The proposal bundles several unestablished claims: one speaker, seven occasions, and seven separate departures. The history only rules out seven distinct utterances at the same time and rules out a display/hearing artifact; it does not imply repeated departures, nor that one person is speaking. A better discriminating question would isolate the speaker structure, e.g. “Do the seven instances represent seven different people saying the line, rather than one person repeating it?” If a final explanation is required, avoid asserting a specific mechanism unless supported: explain only that the sevenfold repetition is an in-story phenomenon, not simultaneous duplicate speech or presentation formatting.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven instances spoken by seven different people?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven utterances spoken by the same person on seven different occasions?"}
review: The proposal is too specific. “Not seven different people” does not establish that one person says all seven lines, and “not at the same time” does not establish seven separate occasions; the repetitions could involve a non-person source, altered chronology, or another in-story mechanism. The history supports an in-story significance, not merely a display/hearing artifact. A safer discriminating question is: “Do the seven repetitions correspond to separate in-story events or moments?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven repetitions correspond to separate in-story events or moments?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are all seven instances spoken by the same person?"}
review: The question is not redundant: “not seven different people” does not establish that all seven are the same person, especially since the repetitions are separate in-story moments. It is a reasonable discriminator, though it may not explain why those moments recur. A stronger follow-up might ask whether the seven events are repetitions involving the same relationship or situation, rather than assuming a single speaker.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events involve the same two people?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the same person speaking the repeated sentence on all seven occasions?"}
review: This is a valid discriminating question: “same two people” does not establish that the speaker is the same person in every event, nor that the listener’s role is fixed. It avoids asserting a mechanism. However, it may be less informative than asking whether the seven events occur in chronological order or whether each repetition follows a separate disappointment by the same person—provided that distinction is not already covered. Do not infer that the repetition is literal dialogue, since the “same two people” answer could describe separate encounters, memories, or other scenes.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events presented in chronological order?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"In each of the seven events, is the person saying the repeated line speaking directly to the narrator?"}
review: The question is reasonable but assumes the narrator is one of the two people and that each event has a clearly identifiable speaker. Neither is established; the history only says the events involve the same two people. A cleaner discriminating question is: “Across all seven events, is the repeated line addressed to the same person?” This tests the relationship without presupposing that person is the narrator.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Across all seven events, is the repeated line addressed to the same person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"In each of the seven events, does the speaker return to the same person after previously saying they would never come back?"}
review: The question is reasonable, but it embeds an unsupported interpretation: that the speaker actually returns after each prior declaration. The history establishes seven separate events involving the same two people and the same addressee, not that each event repeats a return pattern. A cleaner discriminating question would be: “Do the seven events form a recurring cycle in which the speaker leaves and later returns to the same person?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events form a recurring cycle in which the speaker leaves and later returns to the same person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the speaker the same individual in all seven events?"}
review: This is a useful, genuinely discriminating question. “The same two people” establishes the pair, but not whether speaker and addressee keep the same roles in every event; the speaker could alternate. The question should clarify that role assignment, without presuming a mechanism. If answered yes, a later question can investigate what changes between events; if no, test whether the two people alternate roles.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the same individual the speaker in all seven events?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the speaker a child addressing a parent?"}
review: The proposal is unsupported: nothing in the history establishes age or a parent–child relationship. It also risks conflating “same two people” with a particular social role. A safer discriminating question is: “Are the two people related as parent and child?” If that is true, a later question can establish which one is the speaker and whether the seven events reflect repeated disappointments, rather than assuming those details now.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the two people related as parent and child?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"In each of the seven events, does the speaker actually leave the other person immediately after saying the line?}"}
review: The proposed question is too leading: “actually leave” and especially “immediately” assume a departure mechanism not established by the history. It also risks revisiting the rejected recurring-leave/return framing. A better discriminator is: “In each event, does something materially different happen after the line is spoken, rather than the seven events being identical repetitions?” This tests the events’ significance without presupposing what the speaker does. The confirmed facts support only seven separate events involving the same two people, with the same speaker addressing the same person; they do not yet establish departures, returns, or a specific cause.
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each event, does something materially different happen after the line is spoken, rather than the seven events being identical repetitions?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated line spoken by the same person on seven separate occasions because that person can return after supposedly never coming back?"}
review: The proposed question relies on a return cycle, which has already been rejected: the seven events do not form a recurring leave-and-return pattern. “Seven separate occasions” and the same speaker are supported, but the reason for supposedly returning is not. A better discriminating question is: “Do the seven occasions differ in what happens before the repeated line, even though what follows is identical?” Any final explanation should preserve only the established facts: one speaker addresses the same person on seven distinct occasions, with the repetitions significant in-story, but not necessarily because of literal returns.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven occasions differ in what happens before the repeated line, even though what follows is identical?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events connected to the speaker receiving seven separate warnings, reprimands, or punishments from the same person?"}
review: The proposal bundles three different mechanisms—warnings, reprimands, and punishments—so a “yes” would not identify the story’s structure. Nothing so far supports any of them; the history only establishes seven separate events involving the same speaker and addressee, with identical consequences (and rules out a display artifact, simultaneous utterances, a return cycle, and parent-child relation). Ask a cleaner question such as: “In each of the seven events, does the speaker’s action or situation directly cause the same person to say this line?” This tests a repeated causal pattern without presupposing a particular type of reprimand.
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each of the seven events, does something the speaker does directly cause the same person to say this line?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events separate attempts by the same speaker to communicate with the same person, with each attempt failing in essentially the same way?"}
review: The proposal overcommits: nothing establishes that these are communication attempts, that they “fail,” or that the failures are essentially identical. The history supports seven separate events involving the same two people, with the same speaker addressing the same person; it rejects a recurring leave-and-return cycle and says the aftermath is not materially different. A better question would avoid inventing a mechanism: “Are the seven events separate occasions in which the same speaker does something that prompts this person’s repeated disappointment?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events separate occasions in which the same speaker does something that prompts this person’s repeated disappointment?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events seven separate occasions on which the speaker meets or interacts with the addressed person?"}
review: This is mostly redundant and slightly over-specific. The history already establishes seven separate in-story events involving the same two people, with the same speaker addressing the same person. “Meets or interacts” adds a claim not supported by the feedback: the events could be recordings, observations, memories, or other situations without a direct meeting. Also, the rejected hypotheses rule out a recurring leave-and-return cycle and a speaker action prompting the line, so avoid steering toward another ordinary interaction scenario. A better discriminating question would ask about the structure that makes seven distinct events occur—e.g., whether the same speaker addresses the person in seven different settings or circumstances—without presuming physical contact.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events occur in seven different settings or circumstances, despite involving the same two people?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events connected to the same speaker repeatedly failing or making mistakes in a recurring task or test?"}
review: This is weakly supported and partly overlaps rejected directions. The history already says the seven events are not occasions where the speaker does something that prompts the other person’s disappointment, nor does the speaker’s action directly cause the line. A “repeatedly failing or making mistakes” task would normally be exactly such a cause, so this risks rephrasing a rejected hypothesis. It also assumes a recurring task/test without evidence. Ask instead about a structural feature of the seven events that can explain why the same speaker says the same line to the same person, without presupposing failure or causation.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events alternative versions of the same situation, rather than events that all occur in one continuous reality?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events connected because the speaker experiences seven separate deaths or near-deaths, with the other person saying the line each time?"}
review: The proposal reverses an established fact: the same individual is the speaker in all seven events, so it is unsupported to say the other person says the line. “Seven deaths or near-deaths” is also a specific mechanism with no evidence, and the history does not establish that the speaker leaves, returns, or directly causes the disappointment. A better discriminating question would be: “Do the seven events involve the speaker repeatedly being confronted with the same person’s disappointment because of a recurring external circumstance, rather than because the speaker intentionally does something?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the speaker’s repeated disappointment caused by an external circumstance beyond the speaker’s control?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events involve the same speaker repeatedly being placed in, or finding themselves in, a situation where they cannot respond or prevent the other person’s departure?"}
review: The proposal bundles unsupported assumptions: that the speaker is “placed in” the situation, is unable to respond or prevent anything, and that the other person actually departs. The line only asserts disappointment and an intention not to return; it need not describe a departure. It also risks conflicting with the established “no” to an external circumstance beyond the speaker’s control. A better discriminating question would isolate the key action: “In each event, does the addressed person leave immediately after saying this line?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each event, does the addressed person leave immediately after saying this line?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events seven separate occasions on which the same person dies or otherwise ceases to exist after addressing the speaker? "}
review: The proposal is poorly targeted and ambiguous. Prior history establishes that the repeated line’s speaker is the same individual each time and its addressee is also the same individual; “the same person dies after addressing the speaker” appears to assign the death to the addressee, but does not clearly specify which role. It also introduces “or otherwise ceases to exist,” making the hypothesis unfalsifiably broad. Moreover, the history rejects a recurring leave-and-return cycle and says the repeated events are not alternative versions, while giving no support for death. A better discriminating question would be: “In each event, does the person addressed by the repeated line die immediately afterward?” If that is not answered, the final explanation should avoid death and state only the supported structure: one speaker repeatedly addresses one person across seven distinct events, whose causal relationship and aftermath remain unresolved.
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each of the seven events, does the person addressed by the repeated line die afterward?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated line spoken by the same person on seven separate occasions, with the other person merely hearing or witnessing it rather than being the one who says it?"}
review: The proposal is largely redundant: the history already establishes the same speaker, same addressee, and seven separate events. “Merely hearing or witnessing” is an unsupported extra distinction and makes the question compound. A better discriminating question would be: “Is the addressed person physically present and directly hearing the line in each of the seven events?” If a final explanation is required soon, retain only the established facts and avoid inventing a mechanism for why the events repeat.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the addressed person physically present and directly hearing the line in each of the seven events?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated line spoken by the same person into a recording or communication that the addressed person is not present to hear at the time?"}
review: The proposal is too specific and bundles alternatives: the history only establishes that the addressee is not physically present and directly hearing the line, not that it is recorded or transmitted through a communication. It could instead be written, remembered, overheard, or otherwise represented. Ask a broader discriminating question: “In each event, is the line conveyed indirectly rather than spoken face-to-face to the addressed person?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each event, is the line conveyed indirectly rather than spoken face-to-face to the addressed person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated line written down or otherwise recorded in each event, rather than actually spoken aloud?"}
review: The proposed question is too narrow: “recorded” conflates written text, audio/video recording, and possibly another indirect mechanism, while the history only establishes that the line is not heard face-to-face. It also risks assuming all seven events use the same medium. A better discriminator is: “In each event, does the addressed person encounter the line through a message or artifact left by the same speaker?” This tests indirect transmission without prematurely choosing writing or recording. Any final explanation must preserve that the seven are genuine separate events involving the same two people, not seven simultaneous utterances, display artifacts, different speakers, a recurring leave-and-return cycle, or alternate realities.
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each event, does the addressed person encounter the line through a message or artifact left by the same speaker?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated line occur in seven separate dreams experienced by the addressed person? "}
review: The dream hypothesis is unsupported. The history establishes seven separate events involving the same speaker and addressee, but does not establish that the addressee experiences them, much less while dreaming. “Indirect” was both yes and no, so it should not be treated as evidence for a dream mechanism; the artifact hypothesis was already rejected. Ask a broader discriminating question first: “Are the seven events caused by the addressee’s own mental experiences, rather than by external communications or events?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events caused by the addressee’s own mental experiences, rather than by external communications or events?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events repetitions of the same speaker receiving the same recorded or broadcast message from the addressee?"}
review: The proposal reverses the established roles: the same individual is the speaker in all seven events, and the line is addressed to the same person. Asking whether that speaker receives a message “from the addressee” therefore conflicts with the history unless “speaker” is being used differently. “Recorded or broadcast” is also an unsupported pair of mechanisms, and the mixed indirect-feedback does not establish either. A better discriminating question would preserve the roles and test a broader possibility: “In each event, does the same speaker convey the line indirectly through a medium that is not a message or artifact left for the addressee?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"In each event, does the same speaker convey the line indirectly through a medium that is not a message or artifact left for the addressee?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven separate events occur within dreams experienced by the same speaker?"}
review: The proposal is weakly supported and may conflict with the history. The seven events occur in one continuous reality (not alternatives), but nothing establishes that they are dreams, or that the same speaker experiences them. “Are the seven events caused by the addressee’s own mental experiences?” was already answered no; while this asks about the speaker’s dreams, it still assumes a mental-experience mechanism without evidence. The prior answers instead suggest indirect conveyance, but explicitly rule out messages/artifacts and a medium that is not a message or artifact—possibly indicating a more specific ordinary situation rather than dreams. A better discriminating question would avoid presuming dreams: “Are the seven events scenes represented in some physical or recorded medium that the addressee encounters?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events occur as parts of a single recorded or performed work that the addressee experiences?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Do the seven events occur during the same continuous real-world period of the speaker’s life?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable but low-yield: “same continuous real-world period” is vague and does not distinguish whether the seven events are temporally separated, simultaneous in some unusual sense, or parts of one situation. It also risks revisiting chronology, already marked irrelevant, without addressing the stronger constraints: the events are distinct, occur in one reality, involve the same speaker and addressee, and are not a leave/return cycle, artifact, mental experience, or recorded/performed work. A better question would target the unresolved structure: “Are the seven events distinct repetitions within one overarching in-story situation, rather than seven independently motivated occasions?” If forced to finalize, explain only that one speaker repeatedly indirectly conveys the same disappointment to the same person across seven real events; do not assert a specific medium or mechanism, since the feedback has not established one.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events distinct repetitions within one overarching in-story situation?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated line spoken by a human character within the story?"}
review: The question is not redundant, but it is underspecified: “within the story” and “human character” leave unclear whether it asks about the original speaker, an intermediary, or the addressee’s experience. It also may conflate being spoken with being presented indirectly, which has already received mixed (“yes and no”) feedback. A sharper discriminating question would be: “Are the seven instances caused by the same speaker repeatedly producing the line in a single overarching situation, rather than by seven separate speakers or communications?” However, much of that is already established: one speaker, one addressee, seven separate events, and one overarching situation. Consider instead asking about the unresolved medium or structure without presupposing a mechanism, e.g. “Are the seven events repetitions of a performance or action occurring within the same in-story situation?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven events repetitions of the same performance or action within the single overarching situation?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Are the seven repetitions caused by the same speaker repeatedly attempting the same task or action and failing each time?"}
review: The proposal overcommits: “same task,” repeated attempts, and failure are not established. The confirmed pattern is seven repetitions of the same performance/action within one overarching situation, involving the same two people; the repetition is in-story, but not seven simultaneous utterances, separate settings, a recording, an artifact, or a recurring leave-and-return cycle. Ask instead: “Within the single situation, are the seven repetitions caused by the same speaker performing the same action seven times, with the line occurring as part of that action?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Within the single situation, are the seven repetitions caused by the same speaker performing the same action seven times, with the line occurring as part of that action?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated action a physical action performed by the speaker, rather than speaking, writing, or thinking?"}
review: The question is reasonably discriminating, but it assumes “the repeated action” can be cleanly separated from speaking. The line is part of the same repeated performance/action, yet the history does not establish whether it is spoken aloud, prerecorded, or otherwise produced. Also, “physical” versus “speaking, writing, or thinking” is not exhaustive and may conflate the action with the line’s medium. A better question would be: “Is the repeated action primarily a visible bodily action performed seven times by the same speaker, with the quoted line spoken during each repetition?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the repeated action primarily a visible bodily action performed seven times by the same speaker?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve the speaker physically striking or hitting something?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable but somewhat narrow: “striking or hitting” assumes forceful impact and may miss actions such as pressing, knocking, or repeated gestures. No prior answer specifically supports impact; the history only establishes a visible bodily action performed seven times in one situation, with the line recurring as part of it. A better discriminating question is: “Does the repeated bodily action involve the speaker making physical contact with another person or object?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve the speaker making physical contact with another person or object?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve striking or hitting an object?"}
review: The question is permissible but prematurely narrows “physical contact” to striking an object; the action could involve contacting a person, or touching/manipulating rather than hitting. A better discriminating question is: “Does the repeated action involve the speaker physically contacting another person?” This cleanly separates the two possibilities already established without assuming that contact is a blow.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker physically contacting another person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve knocking on or striking a door?"}
review: The proposal is plausible but bundles two unsupported assumptions: that the object is a door and that contact is specifically knocking/striking. The history establishes only repeated bodily contact with an object, not its identity or the kind of contact. A cleaner discriminating question is: “Is the object being contacted a door?” If yes, follow up on whether the action is knocking, opening, closing, or something else.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object being contacted a door?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve the speaker striking or hitting the object?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable and not directly repeated, but “striking or hitting” may be too narrow: the action could involve knocking, tapping, pressing, or otherwise contacting the object. A more discriminating version is: “Does the speaker contact the object by hitting, tapping, or knocking on it?” This preserves the established bodily-contact premise without assuming forceful impact.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the speaker contact the object by hitting, tapping, or knocking on it?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated bodily action involve the speaker opening or closing the object?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable, but “opening or closing” combines two distinct hypotheses, so a yes would not identify which action is involved. The history only establishes repeated bodily contact with an object, while ruling out a door and hitting/tapping/knocking; it does not support assuming the object is operated by opening or closing. Ask instead: “Does the speaker open the object seven times?” If no, a follow-up can test closing. Also remember that the repeated line may be indirect or otherwise part of the action—the mixed feedback does not establish a specific mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the speaker open the object seven times?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object contacted by the speaker a ball?"}
review: The ball hypothesis is currently unsupported: nothing in the history indicates a game, sport, or spherical object. It is a permissible test, but it is quite narrow and may waste a turn. A better discriminating question is: “Is the contacted object something normally used in a game or sport?” This tests the broader category without presupposing a ball. Note that the failed “hitting, tapping, or knocking” question does not rule out every kind of contact (such as kicking, catching, or brushing).
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the contacted object something normally used in a game or sport?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the contacted object a musical instrument?"}
review: The musical-instrument question is plausible but too specific: nothing established that the object produces music or is designed as an instrument. It also risks overlooking ordinary objects contacted through a performance. A better discriminating question is: “Does the repeated contact produce an audible sound from the object?” This tests a meaningful property while covering instruments and other possibilities. No prior question directly establishes sound, and the rejected hypotheses do not rule it out.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated contact produce an audible sound from the object?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the contacted object a button or switch that the speaker activates seven times?"}
review: The proposal is plausible but too narrow: nothing establishes that the object is a button/switch or that contact means activation. The “no” answers rule out several contact types, but do not uniquely support a control. Ask a broader discriminating question, such as: “Does the repeated contact involve pressing the object with a finger?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated contact involve pressing the object with a finger?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker using their foot to contact the object?"}
review: The proposed question is supported by the history: contact with an object and no finger-pressing, knocking, opening, door, sport/game, or person-contact have been established. Foot contact remains untested and could discriminate among bodily actions. However, it assumes the relevant contact is specifically with a foot; a “no” would not meaningfully narrow all remaining possibilities. It is still a reasonable next question, provided it is not treated as evidence for any particular object or mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker kicking the object?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker throwing the object?"}
review: The question is permissible and not already asked, but it is only a weak discriminator: it presumes the contacted object is throwable and still leaves unexplained how throwing produces the repeated line. The history establishes seven visible contacts with an object by the same speaker, while ruling out several obvious actions, but does not establish that the object is moved through the air. A stronger question would test the action’s immediate physical result, such as: “Does the repeated action cause the object to change position each time?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action cause the object to change position each time?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker throwing the contacted object?"}
review: The proposed question is not contradicted by prior feedback, but “throwing” is a fairly specific mechanism. The history establishes only that the speaker visibly contacts a non-person object and causes it to change position; it does not establish that the object leaves the speaker’s hand or travels through the air. A better discriminating question is: “Does the object leave the speaker’s hand and travel through the air during each repetition?” This distinguishes throwing from other possible movements such as pushing, sliding, or dropping.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the object leave the speaker’s hand and travel through the air during each repetition?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the contacted object a movable part of a larger machine or device, which the speaker shifts back and forth seven times?"}
review: The proposal is somewhat over-specified: nothing establishes that the object is part of a machine, nor that it is shifted specifically “back and forth.” The known facts only support a bodily contact that repeatedly changes an object’s position, without hand-to-air travel. Ask a cleaner discriminating question: “Is the contacted object a component of a larger device or machine?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the contacted object a component of a larger device or machine?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the repeated action involve the speaker pushing or pulling the contacted object so that it moves along a surface?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable and not directly repeated, but it bundles two mechanisms (pushing and pulling) and assumes the object moves along a surface. The history only establishes bodily contact, object position changes, no throwing, opening, finger-pressing, kicking, door, game/sport object, or machine component; it does not establish the direction or manner of force. A cleaner discriminating question would be: “Does the speaker move the contacted object by sliding it along a surface?” This tests the surface-motion hypothesis without presuming pushing versus pulling.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Does the speaker move the contacted object by sliding it along a surface?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Does the speaker slide a sheet of paper or similar flat item across a surface seven times?"}
review: The proposed question is too specific: the history supports only that the same speaker slides a contacted object along a surface seven times. Nothing establishes that the object is paper, sheet-like, or even flat. Ask a broader discriminator such as: “Is the object flat and flexible?” If yes, paper-like possibilities can be explored; if no, they are ruled out without embedding an unsupported mechanism. Also, “seven times” is already established, so that part adds little.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object flat and flexible?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object being slid a chess piece on a board?"}
review: The chess-piece hypothesis is unsupported: the history already rules out an object normally used in a game or sport, making chess especially unlikely. It also assumes the object is a piece rather than merely something slid along a surface. A better discriminating question would be: “Is the object being slid one of several similar objects arranged on the same surface?” This tests the board-game-like structure without presupposing chess, though note the prior “game or sport” answer may already make that avenue unpromising.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object being slid one of several similar objects arranged on the same surface?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object being slid a piece of furniture?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable, but “piece of furniture” may be too broad and does not follow strongly from the history: the object is merely non-flat/non-flexible, not part of a machine, and slides along a surface. It could be many movable objects. A sharper discriminator would be: “Is the object a chair or other item people ordinarily sit on?” If retaining the furniture question, avoid treating a “yes” as identifying the object or mechanism; it would only establish a category.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object a chair or another item that people ordinarily sit on?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Is the object being slid a game piece on a board, with the seven repetitions representing moves in a board game?"}
review: The proposal is poorly supported and partly conflicts with the history: “Is the object normally used in a game or sport?” was already answered no. A board-game piece is ordinarily used in a game, so this specific hypothesis is effectively rejected.
